extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and general readers interested in procedural law
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, definitions, and procedural requirements governing ex parte legal proceedings (hearings or orders issued in the absence of one or more parties) across common-law jurisdictions, with jurisdiction-specific rules and exceptions described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ex parte
rubrics_metrics.description: In law, ex parte is a Latin term meaning literally 'from/out of the party/faction' and signifies 'on behalf of (name)'. In common law jurisdictions, an ex parte decision is one decided by a judge without requiring all of the parties to the dispute to be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also used to refer to improper unilateral contacts with a court, arbitrator, or represented party without notice to the other party or counsel. In civil law countries the analogous term is inaudita (altera) parte; the precise meaning can vary by jurisdiction and by context (e.g., case captions, agency proceedings such as patent prosecution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian ex parte candour requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where proceedings are heard ex parte, a high degree of candour is required, including full and fair disclosure of facts adverse to the moving party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A failure to make such disclosure is ordinarily sufficient to warrant discharge of such order as might be made. The term can also appear in case names to mean 'on the application of' where prerogative relief is sought, which does not necessarily indicate the absence of other parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. due process limits on ex parte orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability of ex parte orders or decrees from both federal and state courts is sharply limited by the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, which require that a person not be deprived of liberty or property without due process of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice this is interpreted to require adequate notice of the request for judicial relief and an opportunity to be heard; a court order issued on the basis of an ex parte proceeding will necessarily be de bene esse (temporary and interim in nature), and affected persons must be given an opportunity to contest the order before it can be made permanent. There are statutory and court-recognized exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use in emergency/protective orders ('wrecking ball' standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial ex parte civil protection or restraining orders are permitted in many U.S. states where advance notice would allow the respondent to cause irreversible damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly commentary describes ex parte protection orders as appropriate in 'wrecking ball' situations where giving advance notice would enable irreversible harm; typically a second hearing is set shortly thereafter to allow the alleged abuser to answer the allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State court notice and timing requirements (example: California/Illinois)
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts vary, but in some states (for example California and Illinois) ex parte proceedings are available only if notice is given before 10 a.m. the previous court day, or on shorter notice upon a showing of emergency need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many courts hold law and motion hearings in the early morning, this notice is typically confirmed by facsimile although oral notice may be effective. Some courts permit telephonic appearance by opponents; others do not allow oral argument and only consider written papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: California filing and evidentiary requirements for ex parte relief
rubrics_metrics.description: In California, the party who files an ex parte application must file a declaration showing compliance with notice requirements and no relief may be granted absent such declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ex parte application must contain an affirmative actual showing in a declaration based on personal knowledge of 'irreparable harm, immediate danger, or any other statutory basis for granting relief ex parte' (see California Rules of Court 3.1200 et seq., Rule 3.1203, Rule 3.1204, Rule 3.1202).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent ex parte exceptions (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some bodies operate on a permanent ex parte basis, for example the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) which grants the National Security Agency permission to perform certain types of electronic surveillance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such contexts, parties other than the government are not normally permitted to argue in front of the court, although recipients of court orders may have other statutory or post-order avenues to challenge them.
